newsitem.title: GERMANY: German war exhibition opens after protests.
newsitem.headline: German war exhibition opens after protests.

text.p: A controversial exhibition on German army crimes during World War Two opened without incident on Tuesday after a tumultuous night of clashes between conservative local political leaders and demonstrators.

Late on Monday, a group of protesters stormed a meeting of opponents of the exhibition from the local Christian Social Union (CSU) in Munich's town hall, accusing the party of pandering to right-wing extremists.
Police said the demonstrators poured beer over the heads of CSU officials and their guests. There were reports of scuffles and beer glasses being thrown. Twenty four people were detained.
The exhibition, which challenges the notion that ordinary German soliders had nothing to do with Nazi excesses during World War Two, stirred debate when it was unveiled in Hamburg two years ago.
But it had provoked little controversy since then until the CSU in conservative Bavaria mounted a campaign against it.
Chanting "Honour for the Wehrmacht", backers of the CSU position confronted supporters of the exhibition who gathered outside the town hall shouting "Get out Nazis".
"It's time to put this all behind us," said one opponent of the exhibition. "We weren't the only ones who committed war crimes."

Another participant, who declined to provide his name, said he had spent years studying World War Two and had come to the conclusion that pictures depicting German soldiers committing atrocities were fakes. "I am certain of that," he said.

"The fact is that millions of Jews were killed by the German army," retorted a pro-exhibition demonstrator, only to be told by an older opponent: "I was there, and we didn't know a thing about this (atrocities)."
Jan Philip Reemstma, the exhibition's sponsor, said the controversy in Munich -- which had the status of "Capital city of the Movement" during the Nazi era -- was a sobering experience.
"The reaction throws a interesting light onto the condition of our society," he said at the exhibition's opening ceremony.

The exhibition uses photographs and letters from soldiers themselves to back up its premise that the regular army participated in mass killings of Jews and other atrocities, as well as the SS units usually blamed for war crimes.
The organiser of the exhibition, historian Hannes Heer, said the CSU was trying to challenge "undisputed historical facts".
Heer said the Wehrmacht was the second pillar of Hitler's violent regime and was responsible for millions of deaths, although that did not mean every soldier was a war criminal.
